prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS)

Data Collection Status
Active
Frequency
Annual
Latest Data Available
2024
Data Experts
Rachel Morgan, PhD, BJS Statistician
Rebecca Bielamowicz, PhD, BJS Statistician
Emilie Coen, DrPH, BJS Statistician
Susannah Tapp, PhD, BJS Statistician
Alexandra Thompson, BJS Statistician
Erin Tinney, PhD, BJS Statistician
Jennifer Truman, PhD, BJS Statistician
Collection Period

1973–2024

Description

The BJS National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) is the nation's primary source of information on criminal victimization. Each year, data are obtained from a nationally representative sample of about 240,000 persons in about 150,000 households. Persons are interviewed on the frequency, characteristics, and consequences of criminal victimization in the United States. The NCVS collects information on nonfatal personal crimes (i.e., rape or sexual assault, robbery, aggravated and simple assault, and personal larceny) and household property crimes (i.e., burglary/trespassing, motor vehicle theft, and other types of theft) both reported and not reported to the police. Survey respondents provide information about themselves (e.g., age, sex, race and Hispanic origin, marital status, education level, and income) and whether they experienced a victimization. For each victimization incident, the NCVS collects information about the offender (e.g., age, race and Hispanic origin, sex, and victim-offender relationship), characteristics of the crime (e.g., time and place of occurrence, use of weapons, nature of the injury, and economic consequences), whether the crime was reported to police, reasons the crime was or was not reported, and victim experiences with the criminal justice system.

The Bureau of Justice Statistics’ National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) is an annual data collection carried out by the U.S. Census Bureau. The NCVS is a self-reported survey that is administered annually from January 1 to December 31. Annual NCVS estimates are based on the number and characteristics of crimes respondents experienced during the prior 6 months, not including the month in which they were interviewed. Therefore, the 2024 survey covers crimes experienced from July 1, 2023, to November 30, 2024, and March 15, 2024, is the middle of the reference period. Crimes are classified by the year of the survey and not by the year of the crime.

Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity in BJS Data Collections

Description

Sexual orientation and gender identity are central to an individual’s self-concept and influence how people experience and interact with the world. Collecting this demographic information allows BJS to produce a variety of statistical estimates for persons who identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, or transgender. These measures are collected on several BJS data collections, although the approach to measurement can vary depending on the collection and the year of administration:

  • National Crime Victimization Survey
  • National Inmate Survey
  • National Survey of Youth in Custody
  • Survey of Prison Inmates

Sexual orientation has three main components: sexual attraction, sexual behavior, and sexual identity. An individual’s sexual identity refers to how an individual self-identifies as lesbian, gay, bisexual, or straight. BJS survey data collections use sexual identity for measuring sexual orientation to meet the objective of estimating the demographic populations of interest. Sexual attraction or behavior refers to an individual’s attraction to, or engagement in sexual activities with, members of the same sex, the opposite sex, or both sexes. Sexual attraction or behavior does not define a demographic population, and same-sex attraction or behavior does not always coincide with gay, lesbian, or bisexual identity. (See National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. 2022. Measuring Sex, Gender Identity, and Sexual Orientation. Washington, DC: The National Academies Press.)

Gender identity is defined as an individual’s internal sense or perception of their gender, which can be the same as or different from their sex assigned at birth. Cisgender persons are individuals whose gender identity is the same as their sex assigned at birth. Transgender persons are individuals whose gender identity is different from their sex assigned at birth. (See National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. 2022. Measuring Sex, Gender Identity, and Sexual Orientation. Washington, DC: The National Academies Press.)

Survey data collections

The National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) is the nation's primary source of information on criminal victimization. Each year, data are obtained from a nationally representative sample of about 240,000 persons in about 150,000 households. Persons are interviewed on the frequency, characteristics, and consequences of criminal victimization in the United States.

The 2013 Violence Against Women Reauthorization Act, the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr., Hate Crimes Prevention Act, and other federal laws established protections for violent crime victims who identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, or transgender. Dataset title: National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS)
Description: The National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) is the nation's primary source of information on criminal victimization. Each year, data are obtained from a nationally representative sample of about 240,000 persons in about 150,000 households. Persons are interviewed on the frequency, characteristics, and consequences of criminal victimization in the United States.
URL: https://bjs.ojp.gov/data-collection/ncvs

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS): Research Report

## Summary

Your description is accurate. It matches the Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS) text word for word, and the URL works. The page lists the survey as **Active**, collected **Annually**, covering **1973–2024**, with **2024** as the latest data year.

There is one important caveat. The "240,000 persons in 150,000 households" figure describes a typical year. It no longer matches the most recent data, which was collected during a split-sample transition and a sample reduction. Section 1 explains.

Beyond the description, these are the main things to know:
- The survey changed its questionnaire in 2024–25. This is the first full redesign since 1992.
- A new sample design based on the 2020 census starts in 2026.
- In 2025 the questions about respondents' gender identity were removed.
- BJS's budget and staff are under real strain.

---

## 1. Checking the description

| Claim | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| "Nation's primary source of information on criminal victimization" | ✅ BJS's own wording | The FBI also calls the NCVS and its Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) program "the nation's two crime measures." |
| "~240,000 persons in ~150,000 households" each year | ⚠️ True for a typical year only | BJS's 2024 report itself says "in a typical year." In 2024 the sample was split in half. The half that got the old ("legacy") questionnaire produced **109,341 person interviews in 69,396 households**. The 2025 paperwork filing with the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) also describes a **10% cut in sampled housing units**. |
| Interviews on the "frequency, characteristics, and consequences" of victimization | ✅ | |
| URL | ✅ Works | Related pages: the program page at bjs.ojp.gov/programs/ncvs and the dashboard at ncvs.bjs.ojp.gov |

**A nuance worth stating in any catalog record:** households stay in the sample for 3½ years and are interviewed every 6 months, seven times in total. This suggests the annual counts are interviews completed, not unique people. Check this against the technical documentation before treating them as distinct individuals.

---

## 2. Who publishes it

- **Sponsor and publisher:** the Bureau of Justice Statistics, which sits in the Office of Justice Programs (OJP) within the U.S. Department of Justice. BJS is one of the 13 principal federal statistical agencies.
- **Data collector:** the U.S. Census Bureau (Department of Commerce), using its field interviewers.
- **Archive and distributor:** the National Archive of Criminal Justice Data (NACJD), part of ICPSR at the University of Michigan.
- **BJS contacts listed on the page:** statisticians Rachel Morgan, Rebecca Bielamowicz, Emilie Coen, Susannah Tapp, Alexandra Thompson, Erin Tinney, and Jennifer Truman. Truman is also the contact on the OMB filing.
- **Leadership:** BJS has had no confirmed director since August 2023. Kevin M. Scott has been acting head since Alexis Piquero left. The director is a presidential appointee.

## 3. Legal authority and mandate

- **Main statute:** 34 U.S.C. § 10132, from the Justice System Improvement Act of 1979. This is the authority cited on the current OMB approval.
- **OMB approval number:** 1121-0111. The latest approval came on 12/15/2025 and runs to **12/31/2028**. It covers the 2026 sample redesign.
  - Estimated burden: 157,439 responses a year, 123,202 hours, about 34 minutes per interview.
  - Estimated **annual cost to the federal government: $55.1 million.**
- **Hate crime reporting:** 34 U.S.C. § 41305 requires BJS to report hate crime statistics. The NCVS meets this requirement. The 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act shapes the categories used.
- **Use limits:** BJS data may be used only for statistical or research purposes, never for law enforcement. The BJS director page states this. Census Bureau confidentiality rules also apply, so check the user guide for specifics.
- **Participation is voluntary.**
- **Other mandates (from memory, not checked this session):** the Crime Victims with Disabilities Awareness Act of 1998 led to disability measures. The 2013 Violence Against Women Reauthorization Act is cited by BJS as one basis for the sexual orientation and gender identity questions.

## 4. History

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1965–67 | President Johnson's Commission on Law Enforcement and Administration of Justice ran a pilot survey of 10,000 households. It found a large gap between crimes victims experienced and crimes reported to police, and recommended a continuous survey. Its report was *The Challenge of Crime in a Free Society*. |
| July 1972 | The Law Enforcement Assistance Administration (LEAA) and the Census Bureau launched the **National Crime Survey (NCS)**. It covered 72,000 households, 15,000 businesses, and 26 large cities. |
| 1973 | First full year of data. The annual "Criminal Victimization" report series begins. |
| 1976 | A National Academy of Sciences review recommended a redesign. The business and city surveys were later dropped. |
| 1979 | LEAA was dissolved and the new BJS took over the survey. A redesign research group led by the Bureau of Social Science Research began work. |
| 1992 | Major redesign. The survey was **renamed the NCVS**, with better questions for detecting victimization, much better measurement of rape and sexual assault, and computer-assisted interviewing. Comparable data series begin in 1993. |
| 2006 | Methodological changes. BJS does not publish 2006 national rates in its trend tables (shown as "--"). |
| 2008 | National Academies report *Surveying Victims*. |
| 2011–12 | Replicate weights added (2011). Repeated "series crimes" counted up to 10 times (2012). |
| 2016 | Sample redesign, with a revised 2016 file so years can be compared. Questions on sexual orientation and gender identity added for respondents aged 16 and older. |
| 2014–2023 | Research to redesign the questionnaire, including the National Survey of Crime and Safety (NSCS) field test run by Westat. Supplements were paused in 2023–24. |
| 2020 | COVID-19 changed field operations, and an extra weighting adjustment was added. |
| 2022–23 | 50th anniversary. A new way of measuring prevalence (the One Victimization Adjustment Method) was adopted starting with the 2023 data. |
| 2024 | Split sample: half the households got the legacy questionnaire, half the redesigned one. |
| 2025 | Fully redesigned questionnaire in use. Gender identity questions removed under Executive Order 14168. |
| 2026 | New sample design based on the 2020 census begins. |

## 5. What the survey covers and how it works

- **Who is surveyed:** people aged 12 and older in U.S. households, including some group housing such as dorms. It excludes people on military bases, in institutions such as prisons or hospitals, and people experiencing homelessness.
- **Crimes covered:** rape or sexual assault, robbery, aggravated and simple assault, personal larceny, burglary or trespassing, motor vehicle theft, and other household theft. It counts crimes **whether or not they were reported to police**.
- **What it does not cover:** homicide, crimes against businesses, and victims under 12.
- **Details collected for each incident:**
  - offender age, sex, race, and relationship to the victim
  - time and place, weapons, and injuries
  - financial losses
  - whether the crime was reported to police, and why or why not
  - the victim's experience with the justice system
- **Sample design:** a two-stage sample. First, metro areas or counties are selected, then housing units within them. Each household gets seven interviews over 3½ years, every 6 months, with a 6-month look-back each time. The first interview is usually in person and later ones in person or by phone.
- **Counting rules:** crimes are assigned to the year of the interview, not the year they happened. The 2024 survey covers crimes from July 2023 through November 2024.
- **Response rates (2024 legacy half):** 60% of eligible households and 81% of eligible people within responding households. Household response has fallen over time, which is an important quality concern.
- **Weights:** files include household, person, incident, and victimization weights, plus replicate weights since 2011. An adjustment for extreme weights was added in 2020.
- **Supplements:**
  - School Crime Supplement (with the National Center for Education Statistics)
  - Police-Public Contact Survey
  - Identity Theft Supplement
  - Supplemental Fraud Survey
  - Supplemental Victimization Survey (stalking)
- **New modules in the redesign:**
  - Police Performance
  - Community Safety
  - Vandalism, newly screened for
  - Expanded questions on sexual assault and on victim services

## 6. Key findings: Criminal Victimization, 2024 (released September 29, 2025)

- Violent victimization: **23.3 per 1,000** people aged 12 and older, about **6.7 million** incidents. That is not significantly different from 2023 (22.5) but above 2020 (16.4) and 2021 (16.5).
- Violent crimes reported to police: 11.2 per 1,000.
- 1.45% of people experienced at least one violent victimization. Among ages 12–17 the share rose to 1.95%.
- The 1993 rate was 79.8, so the long-run decline is roughly 70%.
- Estimates for 2024 are less precise because the sample was split. The 95% confidence interval for the rate runs from 19.8 to 26.8.
- Estimates from the redesigned 2024 questionnaire have not been released yet ("at a later date"), and no release schedule has been set for 2025 data.

## 7. Getting the data

- **Public microdata at ICPSR/NACJD,** free and with no membership required:
  - Concatenated file, legacy version, 1992–2024 (ICPSR 39273): household file about 14 GB, person file about 16 GB, incident file about 4 GB. Available in Stata, SAS, SPSS, R, and delimited ASCII formats.
  - 2024 legacy annual file (ICPSR 39272).
  - Redesigned-questionnaire files are "forthcoming."
  - The smallest public geography is the **Census region**. Data may be used only for statistics and must not be used to identify anyone.
- **BJS tools:** the N-DASH dashboard with standard errors and confidence intervals, the NCVS API (including "NCVS Select" files), and published data tables.
- **Restricted data:** detailed geography generally requires an approved project in a Federal Statistical Research Data Center (from memory, not checked this session).
- **Documentation:** codebooks, user guides, source and accuracy statements, the 2016 technical documentation (NCJ 251442), and the 2024 and 2025 questionnaires.

## 8. Who uses it

- **Data scientists and analysts:** a complex survey design, so use the weights and the replicate weights or the published variance formulas. Trends across the 2006, 2016, and 2024–25 breaks need care.
- **Criminologists and economists:** research on the "dark figure" of crimes never reported to police, victim–offender relationships, cost of crime, and repeat victimization.
- **Federal policymakers and Congress:** Violence Against Women Act oversight, hate crime reporting, and victim services funding.
- **Victim advocates:** domestic and intimate partner violence, sexual assault, why victims don't report, and victims' use of services.
- **Police and local governments:** benchmarking reporting rates and, with the new modules, public views of police.
- **Journalists and fact-checkers:** checking claims about crime trends independently of police-reported data.
- **Educators, through the School Crime Supplement.**

## 9. Benefits to the public

- It is the only national measure of crime **not filtered through police reporting.** In 2024, only about half of violent victimizations were reported to police.
- It complements the FBI's UCR and its National Incident-Based Reporting System (NIBRS). BJS published a comparison of the two in November 2025.
- It offers a consistent series from 1973 to the present, which allows long-run trend analysis.
- It gives the victim's point of view: injuries, financial losses, and dealings with the justice system.
- It includes consistent demographic detail on victims, which supports equity analysis.

## 10. Known limitations

- Recall and "telescoping" errors: respondents may place an incident inside the 6-month window when it actually happened earlier.
- Under-reporting of sensitive crimes, especially in household interviews where others may be present.
- Falling response rates.
- Little geographic detail in the public files.
- Small samples for rare crimes and small groups.
- No homicide, business crime, or crimes against children under 12.
- Breaks in the series in 1992–93, 2006, 2016, 2020 (COVID), and 2024–25, plus the 2026 sample redesign.

## 11. For preservationists and policy advocates

- **Removal of gender identity questions:**
  - In late January 2025, Census Bureau leadership told interviewers to skip gender-related items in the School Crime Supplement. BJS's own memo says this happened before OMB approval.
  - On March 1, 2025, BJS asked OMB to remove the gender identity questions to comply with Executive Order 14168.
  - Hate-crime questions about gender identity were kept after OMB and White House Counsel found they did not conflict with the order. OMB also reminded the agencies that **even a pause or skipped question requires approval** under the Paperwork Reduction Act.
  - **Result:** victimization rates for transgender people cannot be calculated from 2025 onward. Data from 2016–2024 with these questions is a finite resource, so prioritize preserving those files and questionnaires.
  - Similar edits were made to BJS's Survey on Sexual Victimization and Survey of Inmates in Local Jails.
- **Budget and staffing:**
  - The American Statistical Association's 2025 *The Nation's Data at Risk* report rates BJS resources "weak." It cites about a 30% loss of purchasing power since 2018, and the BJS director is a political appointee with no fixed term.
  - The Council on Criminal Justice reports that in FY2024 the NCVS cost more than BJS's entire congressional appropriation.
  - Congress cut BJS and National Institute of Justice funding by **15% for FY2026.**
  - Sample cuts have already happened.
- **Archiving priorities:**
  - BJS cannot update its own website directly, according to the ASA report.
  - Preserve the questionnaires for every year, especially 2016–2024, along with the user guides, codebooks, N-DASH outputs, API extracts, and the methodology reports on the redesign and split sample.
  - ICPSR holds the microdata at a university, outside the government, which offers some protection.
- **What to watch:**
  - release of the redesigned-questionnaire 2024 data and the 2025 data
  - whether the supplements resume (planned for 2025)
  - BJS's annual release calendar and any changes to it
  - the 2026 sample redesign
  - nomination of a BJS director

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

# NCVS Risk Assessment

These levels reflect what I could find as of early October 2026. The two biggest problems are a missed fall 2026 release and a 2025 question change ordered by a presidential executive order. The NCVS's legal footing is strong and its past data is intact. Its budget, staff and leadership are under steady strain but haven't hit the "High Risk" thresholds.

**Correcting my earlier report:** I said Congress cut BJS funding 15% for FY2026. That figure is for the shared Justice Department research and statistics budget (BJS plus the National Institute of Justice, NIJ). BJS's own direct appropriation fell 5.7%, from $35M to $33M.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability: **No Known Issue**

**Points toward higher risk:**
- The gender identity questions were dropped from 2025 onward. That changes future collection, not the existing files.
- The public data series already has known methodological breaks (1992–93, 2006, 2016, 2024). These are documented design changes, not removals.

**Points toward No Known Issue:**
- The combined 1992–2024 microdata (ICPSR study 39273) and the 2024 annual file (ICPSR 39272) are still online at ICPSR's criminal justice archive, which is run by the University of Michigan, outside the government.
- The BJS data page, the dashboard (updated 10/5/2026) and the published tables still cover 1993–2024.
- BJS's page on sexual orientation and gender identity questions is still live. It describes the 2016 addition of those questions to the NCVS.
- In July 2026 BJS *added* data, releasing the redesign field-test files through ICPSR.

**Why this level:** I found no evidence that past files or variables were removed or altered. One limit: I didn't check variable by variable that the 2016–2024 gender identity items are still in the public or restricted files. Preservationists should check this and keep copies.

## 2. Future Data Availability: **Moderate Risk**

**Points toward High Risk:**
- BJS normally publishes its annual "Criminal Victimization" report in the fall after collection, and the 2024 report came out in September 2025. BJS's 2026 schedule of upcoming publications does not list "Criminal Victimization, 2025" for any quarter. The dashboard still shows 2024 as the latest year.
- Estimates from the half of the 2024 sample that used the new questionnaire were promised "at a later date." More than a year later, they still haven't appeared.
- BJS's redesign page says release timelines "will be developed following the completion of data processing."

**Points toward Moderate Risk:**
- The usual release date has been missed and there is no new date. But there is no announcement that the release is cancelled or skipped.

**Points toward No Known Issue:**
- The OMB approval for the survey (1121-0111) is active through 12/31/2028. It was renewed on 12/15/2025, before the 11/30/2026 expiration, after the required public notices (90 FR 34884 in July 2025 and 90 FR 47384 in October 2025).
- Collection continues, with the new questionnaire fully in use in 2025 and a new sample design in 2026.

**Why this level:** The publication is late with no schedule, but collection is continuing under a valid approval. No statutory deadline has been missed and nothing has been formally skipped. If 2025 estimates don't appear by 2027, this should move to High Risk.

## 3. Data Quality: **High Risk**

**Points toward High Risk:**
- **Smaller sample:** OMB's approval records a "10% reduction in the number of sampled housing units." Expected responses fall from 180,831 to 157,439 a year, a 13% drop.
- **Less detail:** gender identity questions were removed in 2025, so rates for transgender people can no longer be calculated.
- **Less precision:** 2024 estimates rest on half a sample (109,341 people interviewed), which widens confidence intervals.
- **Supplements stopped:** none of the five supplements (school crime, police contact, identity theft, fraud, stalking) ran in 2023 or 2024. I found no confirmation they resumed.
- **Slower releases:** the 2025 report and the 2024 redesigned-questionnaire estimates are both late (see section 2).
- In an April 2026 letter, research groups wrote that the NCVS "has been forced to reduce its sample size" and that BJS can't sustain it without "significantly compromising other BJS activities."

**Points toward Moderate or No Known Issue:**
- The redesign improves how crimes are measured and adds modules on police performance and community safety.
- The 2026 sample update brings the design in line with the 2020 census.

**Why this level:** Detail, precision and timeliness have all measurably declined. These are current reductions, not just risks on the horizon.

## 4. Statutory Context: **No Known Issue**

**Points toward higher risk:**
- The main law (34 U.S.C. § 10132) authorizes collecting victimization statistics but doesn't spell out survey design, sample size or how often to collect.
- The FBI's crime reporting programs (Uniform Crime Reporting and its incident-based system, NIBRS) partly overlap.

**Points toward No Known Issue:**
- § 10132 explicitly directs BJS to collect and analyze information on criminal victimization. It is the authorizing law cited in OMB's approval.
- 34 U.S.C. § 41305 requires hate crime statistics, which the NCVS supplies.
- Congress actively engages with it: the Senate's FY2026 appropriations report repeated its directive that BJS collect NCVS data on offenders' substance use.
- **No real substitute exists.** FBI data counts only crimes reported to police, and about half of violent victimizations go unreported. BJS itself calls the two programs complementary.

**Why this level:** The legal mandate is explicit and nothing can replace this data.

## 5. Staffing and Funding: **Moderate Risk**

**Points toward High Risk:**
- The FY2026 law cut the combined BJS and NIJ appropriations about 15% from FY2025 (Council on Criminal Justice). NIJ took most of it (26.7%).
- BJS's FY2024 budget of about $59M was below the roughly $62M needed to run the NCVS alone (American Statistical Association, ASA).

**Points toward Moderate Risk:**
- **Staff:** ASA estimated BJS lost about 14% of staff after FY2024. Its 2026 midyear update puts BJS in the 14–20% loss range.
- **Budget:** BJS's direct appropriation fell 5.7% ($35M to $33M), its lowest level since 2005. Including inflation, BJS has lost nearly 30% of its purchasing power since 2018.
- **Leadership:** BJS has had no permanent director for about three years (Government Executive, July 2026). A Justice Department plan to fold its grant-making office (the Office of Justice Programs, where BJS sits) into a new "Bureau of Justice Grants," with shared administrative services, adds uncertainty.

**Points toward No Known Issue:**
- Hiring has resumed at some statistical agencies.
- No direct budget cut to BJS of 10% or more has been documented.

**Why this level:** Staff losses fall in the 10–39% band and leadership is unstable, but BJS's own cuts are below the 20% High Risk threshold. One gap: the federal staffing tracker you suggested loads its data through JavaScript I couldn't read, and it stopped updating on 12/31/2025. So I relied on ASA's figures.

## 6. Policy: **High Risk**

**Points toward High Risk:**
- **An OMB filing driven by a presidential order:** On March 1, 2025, BJS asked OMB to remove the NCVS gender identity questions to comply with Executive Order 14168 (filing 202503-1121-002). ASA confirmed this, along with matching changes to the School Crime Supplement and two surveys of inmates.
- The Census Bureau told interviewers to skip gender items in the school crime supplement *before* OMB approved the change. That bypassed the normal approval process.
- Related BJS actions under other executive orders include cancelling the National Law Enforcement Accountability Database report in January 2025.

**Points toward Moderate Risk:**
- The White House budget request for FY2026 proposed deeper cuts to BJS, and its FY2027 plans remain uncertain.
- The grant-office reorganization is pending.

**Points toward No Known Issue:**
- The survey was not cancelled.
- Hate crime questions about gender identity were kept.
- No negative notice about the dataset appears on BJS's site.

**Why this level:** Changing what the survey asks because of an executive order matches the rubric's "Presidential Action-driven ICR" criterion exactly.
